query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In bulk HfNbTaTiZr, an integrated predictive approach that couples actively‐learned machine‐learning interatomic potentials with extensive Monte Carlo sampling of realistic defect and oxygen impurity configurations will yield electrical conductivity predictions that substantially improve over standard analytical models based on perfect crystals. In particular, the approach will capture the enhanced electron scattering due to defect structures (including oxygen-induced clusters) so that (a) in the cryogenic regime (0–200 K) the predicted conductivity will be significantly lower than defect‐free estimates and (b) in the high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) the predictions will align more closely with measurements on samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr cast as a single-phase BCC solid solution with an inherent defect population and with controlled oxygen impurities up to 1 wt.%.
generation.intervention: Employ a predictive simulation scheme that combines actively learned ML interatomic potentials (trained on ab initio data) with Monte Carlo sampling of defect configurations (including oxygen-induced clustering and lattice distortions) to explicitly incorporate the effect of non-ideal microstructures into conductivity calculations.
generation.conditions: Two temperature regimes are considered: cryogenic temperatures (0–200 K) where defect scattering dominates electron transport, and elevated temperatures (300–1200 K) where both phonon and defect scattering contribute. The method is applied to bulk samples with controlled oxygen levels (both near 0 and ~1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.structural_mediator: Realistic atomic-scale defect distributions including dislocations, vacancy-type defects, and oxygen-induced clusters that induce local lattice distortions, which in turn modulate electron scattering rates.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating the effects of microstructural imperfections and oxygen impurities, the method adjusts the electronic density of states and scattering rates as a function of temperature. At low temperatures, the presence of static defects and oxygen clusters increases electron scattering (reducing conductivity relative to defect‐free predictions), while at high temperatures, thermal vibrations add to scattering but the defect-induced contribution remains non-negligible. This integrated approach overcomes the limitations of analytical methods that assume ideal crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach will predict cryogenic electrical conductivity values that are substantially lower (by a factor of several, e.g. approaching an order of magnitude reduction relative to perfect-crystal models) and high-temperature conductivity values that deviate less from experimental results (with prediction errors reduced to within roughly 50%). Consequently, the model will provide conductivity vs. temperature curves that more faithfully reproduce the measured trends in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical models based on the ideal, defect-free BCC crystal structure, which typically overestimate electrical conductivity—especially at cryogenic temperatures—and do not account for oxygen-induced scattering effects.
generation.boundary: This predictive approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples containing up to ~1 wt.% oxygen and is valid over the temperature ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Its validity may not extend to films or samples with extremely high levels of defects or oxygen beyond the tested range.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from Monte Carlo simulations of HfNbTaTiZr microstructures (PMC7514597::web::012) and improved conductivity predictions in HEAs incorporating plasma frequency and relaxation time (PMC11136967::web::011) support the basic idea, the quantitative effect of defect scattering at cryogenic temperatures and the exact degree of improvement (e.g. the 50% error threshold) remain uncertain. The proposal extends the defect‐aware simulation strategy to conductivity prediction in a system with oxygen contamination—a step not previously tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with near-zero and ~1 wt.% oxygen content. Measure their low-frequency electrical conductivity over two temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) using appropriate cryogenic and high-temperature setups. Simultaneously, run the integrated predictive simulation to generate conductivity vs. temperature curves that include explicit defect and impurity contributions. Compare the predicted and measured conductivity values.
measurements: Electrical conductivity measurements across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K
Characterization of defect density and oxygen distribution (e.g., via microscopy and spectroscopy)
Comparison of simulation-derived conductivity curves with experimental data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the defect-aware predictive approach fails to reduce the prediction error below ~50% relative to experimental data, or if the predicted trends (lower conductivity at cryogenic temperatures relative to perfect-crystal models and convergence at high temperatures) are not observed experimentally, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In conclusion, we have demonstrated how a combination of CPA and actively-learned MTPs can solve the problem of predicting the CRSS and intrinsic ductility of refractory MPEAs over the whole composition space with ab initio accuracy, a problem that is currently not tractable with conventional ab initio-based methods. In particular, by integrating our ab initio automated workflow into a robust Bayesian multi-objective optimization framework we have applied the developed approach to identifying high-performance Pareto-optimal compositions. Furthermore, our supercell size convergence tests enabled by MTP-powered molecular statics have revealed that sizes of typical supercell sizes used in conventional SQS calculations are often insufficient for accurate calculations of certain important materials properties, such as the surface energy, of multi-component alloys. Specifically, the surface energy of MoNbTi has been shown to exhibit a rather slow convergence with the supercell size, which leads to errors of 10–20% for SQS supercells of about 100 atoms.

Very high hardness of the MA-SPS-HPT specimen (584 HV10) can be ascribed to the high oxygen content in solid solution and also the presence of oxide particles that caused additional strengthening. As seen in Figure 8 hardness was correlated with oxygen content in the sample. Hardness remained approximately unchanged with increasing oxygen content up to the oxygen concentration of ≈0.8 wt %. Above this value hardness strongly increased with oxygen concentration. This indicates that there was a certain threshold of oxygen concentration in the sample above which it had a significant hardening effect. It is likely that the remarkable hardening effect of oxygen above 0.8 wt % was connected with the formation of HfO2 particles with a monoclinic structure, which were detected in MA-SPS and MA-SPS-HPT samples by SEM and X-ray diffraction. Additional strengthening (not connected with oxygen) was caused by dislocations introduced by severe (cold) plastic deformation. In Figure 8 one can see that HPT straining increased hardness of both MA-SPS-HPT and AT-SPS-HPT samples.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4.2. Monte Carlo Simulation of Microstructure
cited_evidence.text: Ab-initio MC simulation was performed to evaluate the microstructure stability of investigated alloys. Simulation was performed for the 5 element HfNbTaTiZr alloy, because it contains all elements considered in investigated alloys. Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr ions were distributed randomly in equimolar concentration into a 250 atom BCC supercell. This initial state was relaxed with respect to ion positions until minimum of the total free energy was reached. The equilibrium configuration corresponding to minimum free energy was obtained using a Metropolis MC algorithm at 300 K (room temperature). The details of the simulation and more complete results will be published elsewhere. Figure 7 shows the equilibrium atomic configuration corresponding to the minimum of total energy. The most apparent effect is a rather one-dimensional Ta object (‘wire’) along the <100> direction. The Ta wire is surrounded predominantly by Nb ions. The rest of the simulation box is filled up by the mixture of Ti, Zr and Hf. The latter two elements appear to be well separated from the Ta and Nb region.
